system_overview: This specification models the Chang-Roberts algorithm for leader election in a unidirectional ring network. The algorithm was published by Ernest Chang and Rosemary Roberts in 1979 as 'An improved algorithm for decentralized extrema-finding in circular configurations of processes' (CACM 22(5): 281-283). In this algorithm, processes arranged in a ring each have a unique identifier, and the goal is to elect the process with the smallest identifier among the initiators as the leader.
actors_and_components: The system consists of N processes arranged in a unidirectional ring. Each process has a unique numeric identifier. Each process has a successor (the next process clockwise in the ring); the last process's successor wraps around to the first. Some processes are initiators that begin the election, while others start passively. Processes communicate by passing messages (identifiers) along the ring to their successor.
state_variables: The system tracks: (1) a set of pending messages at each process, representing identifiers that have arrived but not yet been processed; (2) a program counter for each process indicating its current execution phase; (3) whether each process is an initiator (determined nondeterministically at startup); (4) the election state of each process, which can be candidate (still in the running), lost (eliminated from contention), or won (elected as leader).
initial_state: All message sets are empty. Each process nondeterministically decides whether it is an initiator. Initiators begin in the candidate state; non-initiators begin in the lost state. All processes start at the first phase of execution (before sending their initial message).
actions: The algorithm proceeds in two phases per process: (1) Initial send: if the process is an initiator, it sends its own identifier to its successor by adding it to the successor's message set. All processes then move to the main loop phase. (2) Main loop (repeated): the process picks one message (an identifier) from its pending message set and processes it according to its current state: (a) If the process has already lost, it forwards the identifier to its successor unchanged. (b) If the process is still a candidate and the received identifier is smaller than its own identifier, the process marks itself as lost and forwards the received identifier to its successor. (c) If the process is still a candidate and the received identifier is greater than or equal to its own, the message is not forwarded (it is consumed). If the received identifier equals the process's own identifier, the process has won the election and marks itself as the winner.
safety_properties: When any process declares itself the winner: (1) that process must be an initiator, (2) all other processes must be in the lost state, and (3) every other initiator must have a strictly larger identifier than the winner. In other words, the winner is the initiator with the smallest identifier, and the election result is unique and consistent.
liveness_properties: If at least one process is a candidate (i.e., at least one initiator exists), then eventually some process wins the election.
model_bounds: N (the number of processes) is a constant positive natural number. The identifiers are provided as a sequence of N distinct natural numbers. For model checking, typical instantiation uses N equal to 6 with a specific sequence of distinct identifiers.
additional_assumptions: Weak fairness is assumed for each process, ensuring every process eventually takes a step when it is enabled. The algorithm is written in PlusCal and translated to TLA+. The ring is unidirectional: messages can only travel from a process to its successor. The algorithm allows infinite stuttering (self-loops) after all processes have terminated to prevent spurious deadlock detection.
